enough that a business will pay you
money every month for it, forever, is
not cheap, and it is not fast. A
genuinely useful SaaS product, the kind
with real functionality, not a landing
page and a dream, typically takes a
small team of two to five engineers six
months to two years to get to something
customers will actually pay for. At a
fully loaded cost of $150,000
per engineer per year, once you count
salary, benefits, and payroll taxes,
that's easily $300,000
spent before you have a product that
generates a single dollar of revenue.
And that number assumes the first
version works. Most don't. Most SaaS
companies rebuild significant portions
of their product at least once after
learning what customers actually wanted
versus what the founders guessed they
wanted. Then there's infrastructure. And
this is where a lot of first-time SaaS
founders get a nasty surprise. Because
cloud computing bills scale with usage
in ways that are easy to underestimate.
Hosting, databases, and cloud
infrastructure for a small SaaS company
with a modest customer base might run a
few thousand dollars a month. That
sounds trivial. But infrastructure costs
scale with your customers' usage, not
with your revenue. And those two things
don't always move together. A customer
who signs up for your cheapest plan but
uses your product heavily can cost you
more in server load than a customer
paying you 10 times as much who barely
logs in.
Companies building anything involving
artificial intelligence features have
discovered this particularly painfully
in recent years. API costs for large
language model calls can turn what
looked like an 80% gross margin business
into a 40% gross margin business almost
overnight if usage isn't priced and
metered carefully. The classic SaaS
assumption that infrastructure cost is a
rounding error breaks down fast the
moment your product actually gets
popular. Now, here's the part of the
cost structure that catches almost
everyone off guard, and it's not
engineering. It's customer acquisition
cost. And understanding this number is
the single most important skill in
running a SaaS business because it
determines whether growth makes you rich
or bankrupts you. Every SaaS company
spends money to acquire a customer
through paid advertising, sales
salaries, content marketing,
conferences, whatever the channel.
That total spend divided by the number
of new customers it produces is your
customer acquisition cost, or CAC.
Depending on whether you're selling a
$20-a-month tool to individual
freelancers or a $50,000-a-year platform
to enterprise companies, CAC can range
from under $100 to well over $20,000 per
customer. Here's the number that
actually matters, though. The
relationship between CAC and lifetime
value, or LTV, how much total revenue
you'll collect from a customer before
they eventually cancel. The industry
rule of thumb, repeated in every SaaS
finance course, is that you want your
LTV to be at least three times your CAC,
ideally higher. A business where it
costs you $1,000 to acquire a customer
who only ever pays you $800 before
churning out is not a business. It's a
machine for converting investor money
into losses, dressed up in growth
language. This is where SaaS gets
structurally different from a coffee
shop or a gym, and it's worth slowing
down on because it's the entire logic on
underneath every SaaS company's spending
decisions. In most businesses, you have
to make a sale profitable in the same
period you make it. The coffee costs you
a dollar, you sell it for four, you keep
the difference today.
In SaaS, the sale is often unprofitable
the day it happens. You might spend $500
acquiring a customer who pays you $50 a
month. You don't recoup that acquisition
cost until month 10. Everything after
month 10 is where the actual profit
lives, assuming the customer sticks
around that long. This is called the
payback period, and a healthy SaaS
company typically targets recovering CAC
within 12 to 18 months. Push that
payback period out further, and you need
larger and larger amounts of outside
capital just to keep growing because
you're perpetually funding the gap
between spending money to acquire
customers today and collecting enough
from them to break even months or years
from now. Which brings us to the number
that defines whether a SaaS company
survives long enough for any of this
math to matter. Churn. Churn is the
percentage of customers who cancel in a
given period, and it is, without
exaggeration, the single most important
number in this entire business model.
More important than revenue, more
important than growth rate, more
important than almost anything else on
the dashboard. Here's why.
Imagine two SaaS companies, identical in
every way, both adding 100 new customers
a month. Company A loses 2% of its
customer base every month. Company B
loses 8%. That difference sounds small.
It is not small. Run that forward 24
months, and Company A has built a
substantial compounding base of paying
customers, while Company B is running as
fast as it can just to replace the
customers leaking out the bottom, with
almost no net growth to show for all of
that acquisition spending. This is
sometimes called the leaky bucket
problem, and it's one of the most common
reasons SaaS companies with genuinely
impressive-looking new customer numbers
never actually grow their revenue
meaningfully year over year.
A company can be closing new deals
constantly, look busy and successful in
every internal metric that measures
activity, and still be standing still or
shrinking, because the bucket is leaking
faster than it's being filled. Churn
compounds in a particularly unforgiving
way over time, too. A monthly churn rate
of 5% sounds tolerable in isolation.
Compounded over a year, it means you've
lost roughly 46% of the customers you
started with, absent any new sign-ups.
Get that number down to 2% monthly, and
your annual retention looks completely
different. You keep roughly 78% of your
base. That gap between 5% and 2% monthly
churn isn't a rounding error in a
spreadsheet. Over several years, it's
the difference between a company worth
building a career around and a company
that quietly bleeds out, no matter how
good the sales team is. So, how do
successful SaaS companies actually fight
churn? The honest answer is that the
best ones design the entire product and
business around it from day one, not as
an afterthought once customers start
leaving. Onboarding, how quickly and
successfully a new customer gets to
their first real moment of value inside
the product, turns out to be one of the
strongest predictors of whether that
customer sticks around. A customer who
never fully sets up the product, never
connects it to their existing workflow,
never gets a colleague to also start
using it, is a customer who's mentally
already halfway out the door the day
their trial converts to paid. This is
why so many SaaS companies invest
heavily in customer success teams,
product-led onboarding flows, and
integrations with other tools their
customers already use.
Every one of those integrations is, in
effect, a small extra cost the customer
would have to pay in switching effort if
they ever tried to leave, which quietly
reduces churn without ever touching the
price. Now, let's talk about how the
revenue itself is actually structured,
because pricing model decisions here
have consequences that ripple through
the entire business for years. Most SaaS
companies price around a handful of
models: flat monthly or annual
subscriptions, per-seat pricing that
scales with how many people at a
customer's company use the product,
usage-based pricing tied to actual
consumption, or some hybrid combination.
Each of these creates a completely
different revenue growth pattern.
Per-seat pricing is beautifully simple
and predictable, but it caps your
revenue growth at the pace your
customer's own head count grows, and it
can actively work against you if a
customer's business shrinks and they lay
people off. Usage-based pricing can grow
explosively as a customer's usage
scales, which is why it's become popular
with infrastructure and AI-adjacent
products, but it also makes revenue
genuinely harder to forecast because it
depends on customer behavior rather than
a fixed contract number. This is exactly
why so many SaaS companies obsess over a
metric called net revenue retention,
which measures whether your existing
customer base, on its own, is growing or
shrinking in dollar terms. Expansions
and upsells minus downgrades and
cancellations, completely separate from
new customer acquisition. A company with
net revenue retention above 100% is, in
a very real sense, growing even if it
never signs a single new customer
because existing customers are spending
more over time than they're losing to
churn and downgrades. A company below
100% net revenue retention is running on
a treadmill that gets steeper every year
because it has to replace not just
churned customers, but also revenue lost
to downgrades purely to stand still.
Here's a hidden cost structure that
surprises people who assume SaaS margins
are simply high. Support and success
staffing scales with your customer count
in a way that's easy to under budget in
the early excitement of signing new
logos. Every customer, regardless of how
small their monthly payment, generates
support tickets, onboarding questions,
and renewal conversations. A company
that signs a wave of low-priced
customers without proportionally scaling
its support team can find its support
quality collapsing exactly at the moment
churn risk is highest during onboarding
and around renewal time, which creates a
genuinely vicious cycle where cutting
costs to protect margin actually
increases the churn that destroys the
business's long-term value. Sales
compensation is another cost structure
worth understanding, particularly for
SaaS companies selling to larger
businesses rather than individual
consumers. Enterprise sales reps are
typically paid a base salary plus
commission, and a fully loaded
enterprise sales rep, salary,
commission, benefits, travel, the sales
engineering and management support
structure around them, can cost a
company $200,000
a year. That rep needs to close enough
contract value to justify that cost many
times over, which is exactly why
enterprise SaaS deals tend to have long
sales cycles involving multiple
stakeholders, security reviews,
procurement negotiations, and sometimes
months of back and forth before a
contract ever gets signed. A sales cycle
that stretches from an expected 3 months
to 8 months doesn't just delay revenue.
It means that expensive sales rep salary
is being paid for months longer than
budgeted before the deal that justifies
their cost actually closes. Let's talk
about the venture capital layer sitting
on top of a lot of this industry because
it fundamentally shapes how many SaaS
companies actually behave, and it's
worth being honest about the mechanics.
Because SaaS businesses often lose money
for years while acquiring customers,
they frequently raise outside investment
to fund that gap between acquisition
spending and eventual profitability.
That capital comes with an implicit and
sometimes explicit expectation, rapid
growth, because venture investors are
underwriting a portfolio where most
companies fail, and a small number need
to produce enormous returns to make the
math work for the fund overall. This
creates a structural pressure that
doesn't exist in a coffee shop or a gym.
A SaaS company can be perfectly healthy
on a smaller, slower growth trajectory
and still be considered a disappointment
by investors who need outlier outcomes,
which is exactly why so many SaaS
companies chase growth at the expense of
near-term profitability, spending
aggressively on acquisition even when
the underlying unit economics are
marginal, betting that scale and future
price increases will eventually make the
math work. This dynamic produced one of
the most instructive corrections in
recent SaaS history. For years,
particularly through the low interest
rate period of the late 2000s and early
2020s, capital was cheap and plentiful,
and SaaS companies were often valued and
funded primarily on growth rate, with
profitability treated as a problem for
some future year. When interest rates
rose sharply and capital became more
expensive and harder to raise, investor
expectations shifted dramatically toward
efficiency, a metric combining growth
rate and profit margin, sometimes called
the rule of 40, which holds that a
healthy SaaS company's growth rate plus
its profit margin should add up to
roughly 40% or more.
A company growing 60% a year while
losing 30% of revenue is below that bar.
A company growing 25% while running a
20% profit margin clears it comfortably.
That shift in what investors reward
triggered waves of layoffs across the
software industry as companies that had
been optimized purely for growth
scrambled to demonstrate they could also
be run efficiently, sometimes cutting
deeply into the very sales and marketing
spend that had been driving their growth
in the first place. So, let's build the
two honest scenarios for a mid-size SaaS
company because this is where the two
very different versions of this business
reveal themselves. In the optimistic
scenario, you've built a product with
strong retention, a healthy net revenue
retention above 110%, a CAC payback
period under 12 months, and monthly
churn under 2%. Revenue compounds
because you're not just adding new
customers. Your existing base is quietly
expanding through sells and seat growth
even before a single new sale closes. A
SaaS company at $5 million in annual
recurring revenue with these
characteristics can often run gross
margins of 75 to 85% and once it reaches
sufficient scale to spread fixed costs
like engineering and leadership across a
larger revenue base, net profit margins
of 15 to 25% are achievable for a
well-run, efficiently operated company.
That combination, high margins,
compounding retained revenue, and
genuine operating leverage as the
company scales is exactly why software
businesses can eventually generate
returns that dwarf almost any other
industry once they cross the threshold
into sustainable, efficient growth. In
the realistic scenario, a few
unglamorous things go wrong that aren't
exotic at all. They're the normal risks
of this exact business model. Churn
creeps up half a percentage point higher
than modeled because a competitor
launched a genuinely better product and
a wave of contract renewals came due at
the same time. CAC rises because of the
paid advertising channels that used to
work efficiently get more competitive
and more expensive as more SaaS
companies bid for the same keywords. A
key enterprise customer representing 8%
of total revenue doesn't renew because
their own business hit a rough year and
cut software spending. Under those
conditions, a company that looked, on
paper, like it was compounding toward
profitability can find its growth rate
stalling while its burn rate stays
roughly the same, forcing a choice
between raising another round of funding
at a worse valuation than the last one
or making the kind of cost cuts, often
to the very engineering and customer
success teams responsible for product
quality and retention, that can
accelerate the churn problem rather than
solve it. None of this shows up as one
dramatic failure.
It's a slightly higher churn number, a
slightly longer sales cycle, a slightly
more expensive acquisition channel,
compounding quietly month after month
until the metrics on the dashboard look
nothing like the growth story in last
year's pitch deck. So, does owning a
SaaS company actually work as a
business? The honest answer is that it
works spectacularly well for the
companies that get the unglamorous
mechanics right: churn, payback period,
net revenue retention, support scaling.
And it works as an extremely expensive,
slow-motion way to lose other people's
money for the companies that chase
growth while ignoring them. The margins
really are extraordinary once a SaaS
company reaches scale with healthy
retention, but almost nothing about
getting there is as effortless as build
it once, sell it forever makes it sound.
The software is the easy part. The
business underneath it, acquiring
customers efficiently, keeping them long
enough to actually profit from having
acquired them, and building a product
people would genuinely miss if it
disappeared, is where SaaS companies are
actually built or quietly destroyed.

A company that signs a wave of low-priced customers without proportionally scaling its support team can find its support quality collapsing exactly at the moment churn risk is highest during onboarding and around renewal time, which creates a genuinely vicious cycle where cutting costs to protect margin actually increases the churn that destroys the business's long-term value. Sales compensation is another cost structure worth understanding, particularly for SaaS companies selling to larger businesses rather than individual consumers. Enterprise sales reps are typically paid a base salary plus commission, and a fully loaded enterprise sales rep, salary, commission, benefits, travel, the sales engineering and management support structure around them, can cost a company $200,000 to $400,000 a year. That rep needs to close enough contract value to justify that cost many times over, which is exactly why enterprise SaaS deals tend to have long sales cycles involving multiple stakeholders, security reviews, procurement negotiations, and sometimes months of back and forth before a contract ever gets signed. A sales cycle that stretches from an expected 3 months to 8 months doesn't just delay revenue. It means that expensive sales rep salary is being paid for months longer than budgeted before the deal that justifies their cost actually closes. Let's talk about the venture capital layer sitting on top of a lot of this industry because it fundamentally shapes how many SaaS companies actually behave, and it's worth being honest about the mechanics. Because SaaS businesses often lose money for years while acquiring customers, they frequently raise outside investment to fund that gap between acquisition spending and eventual profitability. That capital comes with an implicit and sometimes explicit expectation, rapid growth, because venture investors are underwriting a portfolio where most companies fail, and a small number need to produce enormous returns to make the math work for the fund overall. This creates a structural pressure that doesn't exist in a coffee shop or a gym. A SaaS company can be perfectly healthy on a smaller, slower growth trajectory and still be considered a disappointment by investors who need outlier outcomes, which is exactly why so many SaaS companies chase growth at the expense of near-term profitability, spending aggressively on acquisition even when the underlying unit economics are marginal, betting that scale and future price increases will eventually make the math work. This dynamic produced one of the most instructive corrections in recent SaaS history. For years, particularly through the low interest rate period of the late 2000s and early 2020s, capital was cheap and plentiful, and SaaS companies were often valued and funded primarily on growth rate, with profitability treated as a problem for some future year. When interest rates rose sharply and capital became more expensive and harder to raise, investor expectations shifted dramatically toward efficiency, a metric combining growth rate and profit margin, sometimes called the rule of 40, which holds that a healthy SaaS company's growth rate plus its profit margin should add up to roughly 40% or more. A company growing 60% a year while losing 30% of revenue is below that bar. A company growing 25% while running a 20% profit margin clears it comfortably. That shift in what investors reward triggered waves of layoffs across the software industry as companies that had been optimized purely for growth scrambled to demonstrate they could also be run efficiently, sometimes cutting deeply into the very sales and marketing spend that had been driving their growth in the first place. So, let's build the two honest scenarios for a mid-size SaaS company because this is where the two very different versions of this business reveal themselves. In the optimistic scenario, you've built a product with strong retention, a healthy net revenue retention above 110%, a CAC payback period under 12 months, and monthly churn under 2%. Revenue compounds because you're not just adding new customers. Your existing base is quietly expanding through sells and seat growth even before a single new sale closes. A SaaS company at $5 million in annual recurring revenue with these characteristics can often run gross margins of 75 to 85% and once it reaches sufficient scale to spread fixed costs like engineering and leadership across a larger revenue base, net profit margins of 15 to 25% are achievable for a well-run, efficiently operated company. That combination, high margins, compounding retained revenue, and genuine operating leverage as the company scales is exactly why software businesses can eventually generate returns that dwarf almost any other industry once they cross the threshold into sustainable, efficient growth. In the realistic scenario, a few unglamorous things go wrong that aren't exotic at all. They're the normal risks of this exact business model. Churn creeps up half a percentage point higher than modeled because a competitor launched a genuinely better product and a wave of contract renewals came due at the same time. CAC rises because of the paid advertising channels that used to work efficiently get more competitive and more expensive as more SaaS companies bid for the same keywords. A key enterprise customer representing 8% of total revenue doesn't renew because their own business hit a rough year and cut software spending. Under those conditions, a company that looked, on paper, like it was compounding toward profitability can find its growth rate stalling while its burn rate stays roughly the same, forcing a choice between raising another round of funding at a worse valuation than the last one or making the kind of cost cuts, often to the very engineering and customer success teams responsible for product quality and retention, that can accelerate the churn problem rather than solve it. None of this shows up as one dramatic failure. It's a slightly higher churn number, a slightly longer sales cycle, a slightly more expensive acquisition channel, compounding quietly month after month until the metrics on the dashboard look nothing like the growth story in last year's pitch deck. So, does owning a SaaS company actually work as a business? The honest answer is that it works spectacularly well for the companies that get the unglamorous mechanics right: churn, payback period, net revenue retention, support scaling. And it works as an extremely expensive, slow-motion way to lose other people's money for the companies that chase growth while ignoring them. The margins really are extraordinary once a SaaS company reaches scale with healthy retention, but almost nothing about getting there is as effortless as build it once, sell it forever makes it sound. The software is the easy part. The business underneath it, acquiring customers efficiently, keeping them long enough to actually profit from having acquired them, and building a product people would genuinely miss if it disappeared, is where SaaS companies are actually built or quietly destroyed.

metadata.title: Vertical AI vs Traditional SaaS | Game Over
metadata.author: Bootstrapper's Paradise
metadata.shortDescription:
In February 2026, the software industry experienced a significant market shift as investors recognized the changing landscape, leading to a $1 trillion drop in software stocks. This event highlights the profound ai impact on traditional business models, signaling the collapse of the per-seat pricing saas model. For bootstrap founders, this presents a new playbook and a unique opportunity amidst this business disruption.

In February 2026, $1 trillion was wiped from software stocks in a single week. Not because of recession — because investors realized AI agents don't need software seats. The per-seat pricing model that built the SaaS industry is collapsing. But if you're a bootstrapped founder, this is the best news you've ever heard. Every old rule has changed, and every new rule favors you. Here are the 7 new rules of SaaS in 2026.

Key takeaways:
• Rule 1: Vertical beats Horizontal — vertical SaaS growing at 24% CAGR, nearly 2x the broader market
• Rule 2: Find the buyer first — go-to-market timeline = zero
• Rule 3: AI-native from day one — not a bolt-on, the foundation (80% enterprise adoption by 2026)
• Rule 4: Outcome pricing, not per-seat — the single biggest shift in SaaS history
• Rule 5: Distribution beats Product — founder-led content, email lists, and communities are the moat
• Rule 6: Ship in weeks, stay lean — idea to MVP for under $100, no investors needed
• Rule 7: Context is your moat — CLAUDE.md and domain expertise can't be cloned
• SaaS market: $318B → $576B by 2029 — restructuring, not shrinking
• Micro-SaaS: $5K-$50K MRR with 1-3 people, AI startups at 30x revenue valuations

5:15 -- Rule 5: Distribution beats Product (your real moat)
6:07 -- Rule 6: Ship in weeks, stay lean (under $100 MVP)
7:02 -- Rule 7: Context is your moat (CLAUDE.md)
7:51 -- The numbers: $318B to $576B, micro-SaaS benchmarks
8:54 -- Closing: old rules are dead, new ones favor you

metadata.author: New Machina
metadata.shortDescription:
📹 VIDEO TITLE  📹
What are Vertical Agents?

✍️VIDEO DESCRIPTION ✍️
In this video, we explore the rising concept of “Vertical Agents”, domain-specific AI agents built to handle specialized tasks in industries like healthcare, finance, real estate, customer support, and more. Unlike general-purpose AI assistants, vertical agents are deeply integrated with the tools, workflows, and terminology of a particular field. They’re designed to automate complex tasks, deliver outcomes rather than tools, and interact naturally with both users and systems via APIs and data flows behind the scenes.

We then dive into why many believe vertical agents are poised to “disrupt traditional SaaS” over the next 5 to 10 years. Rather than forcing users to navigate bloated dashboards or learn new interfaces, vertical agents can handle tasks directly through simple prompts or autonomous decision-making. This shift represents a major change—from human-in-the-loop software to agent-driven execution—potentially making many standalone SaaS apps obsolete.

Finally, we discuss how venture capital firms, are betting big on AI-native startups that skip the UI layer and build directly for agentic automation. As industries look for more intelligent, cost-efficient, and integrated solutions, vertical agents offer a compelling alternative to fragmented software stacks. If you're interested in the future of AI and how it's reshaping enterprise software, this is a trend you don’t want to miss.

Well, these emerging vertical agents are designed to replace the need for traditional SAS user interfaces. Vertical agents will actually take on the work for users autonomously or through natural language interaction rather than requiring users to navigate web-based menus, dashboards, and forms. Let me give you a little more detail on the nature of these vertical agents. As I mentioned earlier, they will have a domain specialization. From the start, they will be trained and fine-tuned on domain specific data, language, and workflows. Vertical agents will have high accuracy. So why is this? Well, given that they will operate within a limited domain, they can provide more precise and reliable outputs. They will also have deep integrations into existing domain systems. Vertical agents will include integrations with domain relevant tools or APIs such as electronic health records in healthcare or CRM within a sales organization. And finally, they will be knowledgeable about the respective industry compliance and regulations. They will be built with domain specific regulations in mind such as HIPPA for healthcare or GBA in the financial industry. So what are some examples of vertical agents? Well, in the legal domain, imagine a legal assistant that drafts contracts or summarizes illegal documents. In healthcare, imagine a medical co-pilot that helps doctors interpret patient symptoms and suggests diagnosis. In customer service, imagine a customer service chatbot trained specifically for a telecom company's proprietary support processes. So earlier I hinted that many believe that traditional SAS companies will be replaced by AI native vertically oriented agentic startups over the next 5 to 10 years. So why is this? Well, Agentic systems are outcome oriented. I alluded to this a little bit earlier, but in traditional SAS workflows, a user logs in, clicks buttons, fills in forms, and clicks their way through a cumbersome workflow. With a vertical agentic system, a user interaction will begin with the user asking the agent what it wants it to do and the agent will then go do that for the user. When it comes to getting user adoption, SAS systems come with a learning curve and a training transition. Alternatively, with vertical agentic systems, getting up to speed offers zero friction. Users will simply interact in natural language and let the agent handle the complexity. Regarding integrations with back-end systems and SAS architectures, front ends call APIs which are integrated with back-end logic and databases. Vertical agents are able to use these same existing APIs behind the scenes, minimizing the need for user interfaces altogether. Finally, venture capitalists love to invest when paradigm shifts emerge. If the user interface era of SAS is ending, it opens a new frontier and new opportunities to disrupt the SAS incumbents. Today, AI native venture capitalists are betting that SAS will be disrupted and replaced by vertical AI agents. Okay, so in summary, vertical agents are highly fine-tuned for specific industry verticals such as healthcare, legal, finance, or manufacturing. vertical agents could display SAS incumbents that are slow to adopt this new AI agentic technology. What I can tell you for sure is this. In the next 5 to 10 years, we will all see who ends up as the winners and losers of this technical transition. Let me know what you think of vertical agents. Do you see yourself building a vertical agent near future? Do you see yourself launching a new vertical agentic startup aimed at disrupting a SAS incumbent? If so, let me know in the comments below. I want to hear about it. Okay, thanks for watching. This video along with all the other videos in this playlist are listed in the YouTube description. I invite you to watch other videos on my channel. If you like the way I'm sharing this content, please consider subscribing. When you subscribe, this really helps my channel grow. One last thing, we all love technology and we're all excited about all the innovation with the cloud and machine learning and AI, but don't forget to carve out some time to live in the real world. Go outside, go swimming, go hiking, go climbing, go surfing, but get out and move your body. And if you do, let me know in the comments. I want to hear about it. And with that, have a great day. Thanks. Hey, hey,

metadata.title: AI Is Not Killing Vertical SaaS - It’s Practical Leverage
metadata.author: Practical Founders - with Greg Head
metadata.shortDescription:
Deepak Sindwani is the founder and managing partner of Wavecrest Growth Partners, a growth equity firm focused on bootstrapped, capital-efficient B2B SaaS companies. In this episode, Greg and Deepak break down what actually works for founders who’ve reached $5–$20M in ARR and want to grow without losing control or betting the company on venture math.

They unpack how growth equity really works, how it compares to VC and buyout private equity, and why this stage of company building (from $5M to $50M) is its own sport. Deepak also shares how AI is changing product, go-to-market, and internal operations for practical founder companies—and why vertical SaaS + data moats still matter.

This is a grounded, real-world conversation about scaling profitably, taking some risk off the table, and building durable software companies in today’s market.

Key Takeaways
- Capital Efficiency Matters — Wavecrest only backs profitable or breakeven SaaS companies that already respect the business model fundamentals.

- Founder Liquidity Helps — Taking some money off the table reduces stress and helps founders make better long-term decisions.

- Vertical SaaS Wins — Deep industry knowledge and data create defensibility AI-first competitors struggle to replicate.

- AI Is Additive — Software plus AI and data creates more value than AI replacing SaaS systems of record.

- No One-Size Playbook — Growth equity works best when strategies are customized, not forced by rigid PE-style playbooks.

28:15 – AI’s Real Impact on SaaS
33:55 – Defensibility in Vertical SaaS
36:21 – Go-To-Market Is Changing
40:45 – Exit Paths for Practical Founders
43:01 – Why This Model Still Works

About Practical Founders and Greg Head

Practical Founders build valuable software companies without big VC funding. This growing community of practical founders are winning the startup game with successful exits of $20 million to $100 million for founders, if they ever choose to sell. There has never been a better time to be a practical founder.
 
Greg Head is the founder in chief of Practical Founders. He is a 30-year software industry veteran who was part of the startup-to-scale journeys of three different CRM software companies, including one IPO. He is now an active advisor, community builder, and speaker who helps founders of SaaS software startups worldwide.
 
Greg is a paid strategic advisor to 40 early-stage SaaS company CEOs with his Practical Founders Peer Groups and his 1-1 CEO advisory programs. He hosts the weekly Practical Founders Podcast where he interviews successful founders who grew valuable software companies without big funding.

metadata.title: The Harsh Truth About AI Wrappers (From a Venture Investor)
metadata.author: Indy Pixels | Abdalla Emam
metadata.shortDescription:
The phrase “it’s just an AI wrapper” gets thrown around constantly in startup and venture conversations.

But what do investors actually mean when they say that?

In this episode, Abdalla Emam — Founder & General Partner at Indy Pixels Ventures — breaks down how investors evaluate AI startups today, what actually counts as defensibility, and why many AI products struggle to build long-term value.

We also talk about a growing trend investors are seeing: startups built almost entirely using AI development tools — and why speed alone doesn’t create a durable company.

If you’re building an AI startup, raising capital, or thinking about launching a product in this space, this episode will give you a clearer view of how investors think behind the scenes.

⸻

What You’ll Learn In This Episode

• What investors really mean when they say “AI wrapper”
• The difference between an AI feature and an AI company
• What defensibility in AI actually looks like today
• Why data advantage, workflow integration, and vertical specialization matter
• When starting as a wrapper is actually the right strategy
• The risks of building a startup purely with AI coding tools
• Common pitch mistakes founders make without realizing it
• How the strongest AI companies build compounding advantages over time

⸻

00:30 — AI features vs real AI companies

04:58 — The “no operations needed” misconception
05:23 — Why real customers matter early
05:40 — Building compounding advantages in AI companies
06:00 — How founders can avoid investor red flags

metadata.author: Y Combinator
metadata.shortDescription:
As LLM’s become exponentially better it is clear that vertical AI agents are key to the next generation of billion dollar SaaS companies. In this episode of the Lightcone, the hosts sit down with YC alum Jake Heller, the co-founder and CEO of Casetext (which sold to Thomson Reuters for $650 million in cash in 2023) to discuss what it takes to build a successful vertical AI company and overcome resistance from industry veterans and skeptics.

15:04 Entering deep founder mode
20:40 Approaching prompt engineering step by step
25:05 Going beyond GPT wrappers
28:10 Aiming for 100% accuracy
30:48 Thoughts on o1’s capabilities
36:42 Outro

metadata.title: How to Build a Vertical SaaS Company AI Can’t Replace | Sahill Poddar
metadata.author: Verticals: A Weekly Biz Show On Vertical AI
metadata.shortDescription:
What separates the vertical software companies that compound for decades from the ones that eventually stall?

Sahill Poddar has a unique dataset for answering that question...

In this episode of Verticals, Luke and Nic sit down with Sahil, Co-Founder and CEO of Parafin, the embedded finance infrastructure powering capital products across platforms like DoorDash, Worldpay, and Mindbody. By underwriting the businesses operating across these platforms, Parafin gets a rare look under the hood at what actually separates the strongest vertical software companies from the rest.

We discuss:

-What the best vertical SaaS companies have in common
-Why sequencing matters when expanding beyond your initial wedge
-When vertical software companies should add financial services
-How embedded lending can create stronger retention and higher LTV
-Why AI could turn traditional software platforms into databases

🎟️ TICKETS DROPPED. Vertical Software Summit — 5-billion-dollar Vertical AI CEOs confirmed to speak. Snag a ticket before they're gone: https://verticalsaasgroup.com/conference

🎬 TIMESTAMPS:
00:00 What separates the best vertical SaaS companies
04:56 Why direct SMB lending became a Silicon Valley graveyard
11:16 How a five-person startup landed DoorDash

54:06 Sahill's favorite verticals from 2026

TOPICS

2. Vertical AI & Enterprise Software
3. AI Agents, OpenAI, Anthropic & the Future of SaaS
4. Small Business Finance

metadata.title: What’s the Future of Vertical SaaS in an AGI World? Jamie Cuffe, CEO of Pace
metadata.author: Sequoia Capital
metadata.shortDescription:
Jamie Cuffe is solving one of AI's hardest problems: getting conservative, regulated industries to trust autonomous agents with mission-critical work. At Pace, he's building AI that replaces traditional BPOs in insurance, handling everything from email triage to claims processing with 50-75% cost savings. Drawing on his experience at Retool, Jamie emphasizes the importance of "closing the distance" with customers through forward-deployed engineering and being "the rock" that clients can rely on. He shares how focusing on top-tier insurance carriers and maintaining exceptionally high standards is enabling Pace to capture a meaningful share of the $400 billion BPO market while building a durable business model - at AI-native velocity.

Hosted by Lauren Reeder and Pat Grady, Sequoia Capital

00:00 Introduction 
01:35 The Evolution of Insurance BPOs
04:31 AI's Role in Transforming Insurance
07:58 Building Trust and Success with AI
27:32 Setting the Pace: The Final Principle
28:45 The Bigger Mission: Beyond Insurance
31:06 Transforming the Services Market with AI
35:12 Onsite Implementation and Success Metrics
42:25 Reflections and Advice for AI Founders

metadata.title: The Death of SaaS | Why "Vertical AI" is Taking Over in 2026
metadata.author: BergTube
metadata.shortDescription:
Stop paying for "seats" and start paying for "results." In 2026, the traditional Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) model is dying. We are entering the era of Vertical AI—autonomous agents built specifically for your niche that don't just store data, they perform the work.In this video, we break down:Why "Vertical SaaS" is being replaced by "Outcome-Based" AI.How to identify "Linear Workflows" in your business that can be fully automated.The difference between an AI "Assistant" and an AI "Agent."How to use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to link your tools.A step-by-step guide to reducing your monthly software overhead by 80%.If you’re a solopreneur or agency owner, you can’t afford to stay stuck in the 2024 tech stack. It’s time to build a digital workforce that actually delivers ROI.

Simple, fast, and beginner-friendly.


#Stripe #StripeBilling #UsageBasedBilling #StripeTutorial #SaaS #OnlinePayments #TechTutorial #ThisWorksTutorials

and iterate with evidence rather than
guesswork. That's the full tour.

strategy.

Luckily, with Stripe usagebased billing, we can implement this fairly easily. Why don't we take a look and see how we can get this done? Here, we're looking at the API that we want to monetize. It's a recipes API that allows users to manage their different recipes or even retrieve a random one whenever they need some inspiration. What we want to be able to do is charge users for the amount of requests that they make to this API. Let's head over to our Stripe dashboard and see how we can get this done. In the product catalog, I've gone ahead and set up a product that'll represent the pricing tier for how we're going to charge for these API requests. Notice that this product has two prices. The monthly base price, that's $40 a month, and the API overages that start at $0 a month. Now, this first price, if we take a look at it, is just our standard monthly price that we're going to charge users for having access to the API. The second price represents a tiered pricing model. And if we scroll down to the bottom, you can notice that it's associated with two tiers. The first tier represents a quantity from 1 to 40 and the second tier captures all the rest. So what this means is that for the first 40 API calls, we're not going to be charged any extra to the account. But after we pass that, we're going to be charged 25 cents per additional call that we make to the account. Now to capture the usage, we also had to create what's called a meter. And notice this price is associated with the standard API request meter. So I'm going to click on that. And on the right side you can see some of the various details that you need to start using this meter. Some important information to pay attention to in this section are the event name, the aggregation method, and the payload key. Since the aggregation method is set to sum, what it'll do is add up all of the usage reports that we submit to the Stripe API. Now let's head over to our IDE and generate some requests to see what this looks like. to help me generate some requests. I'm going to have GitHub Copilot help me out a little bit. So, I'm going to add my task file as some context. And this just contains some handy helper methods that I already set up. And now I'm just going to issue a prompt and ask it to call the generate request task 10 times. The script that it generates looks good to me. And I'm going to go ahead and hit continue. And now what it's doing is just running requests against my API. If I head back over to the dashboard, you can see that my meter is starting to collect those usage reports. If we scroll down just a little bit, we can see that the meter is able to identify the customer and also that we're sending usage reports in batches of 10. Now, let's head over to James and see what his subscription looks like. So, we're going to check out James and let's click on his active subscription. So, as we scroll down to the bottom and we go to his invoice in the upcoming invoice, we can see that James has gone above the allotted 40 requests per month and has added an additional 60 on top of that, which is getting charged at 25 cents per request. So now when the next billing cycle comes around, he's going to be charged $55, which includes his monthly base price and the overages from the previous month. Back in our ID, we can see how this was implemented. So, let's close these windows. Now here I have my API controller that has all those different methods. I can open up the get random recipe operation and you can see what I'm doing here is just querying the database for a random record and returning it to the user. So where exactly does the reporting happen? Well, if we head back to the top of our class, you can see that I'm using what's called a service filter. And what the service filter does is allow us to run code before and after each operation is called. So that means before or after I make a call to get random recipe, I can execute some code. Now in this case, I only want to collect the usage report after the operation is completed. And how we do that is by plugging in our code after calling the next delegate in lines 16 through 20. All that we're doing is we're getting the Stripe customer ID from the logged user and using a channel to have the usage aggregated in the background. Next, what happens is that we have a worker that's receiving all those usage reports. So if I open up this execute async method, you can see that I'm reading the messages off the channel and I'm just aggregating them in memory for now. But whenever the usage count gets greater than 10, then I'm just going to make a batch call to send all those usage reports over to Stripe. Now, if we take a look at the report usage batch, what we're doing is collecting all the usage reports and grouping them by user. Then for each user, I'm going to create a meter event and I'm going to specify the name, which in this case is the event name that we saw in those meter details. And in the payload, we supply the customer ID as well as the usage count. So pretty much what this background worker is doing is saying every time I get 10 usage reports, I'm going to send that information over to Stripe. Now, there's one more thing I want to show you inside the dashboard. If we head back over to our customer section, and I'm going to click on James and then the top of the screen, you see that section that says simulation time. And this is because the James Moriati customer is attached to test clock. So, one of the things that we can do is we can use a test clock and advance the time. So, I'm going to say I want to advance this ahead by 1 month. And what that did was simulate the passage of time for James' account. Now, if I scroll down a little bit, I should be able to see James' invoices. And as we move through time, we'll notice that the statuses of these invoices will change. Let's head back to the top and move it forward a few more days. Let's say we advance this like another week. Now, if we head back down and we take a look at our payments, we see that James made a successful payment for that second invoice. And in his invoices section, we'll see that he was able to successfully pay for his two invoices. And this just showed us that using test clocks provides a convenient way for simulating the passage of time whenever we want to validate our usagebased billing scenarios. Hopefully after watching this video, you should feel a little bit more comfortable about implementing usagebased billing inside of your ASP.NET Corebased web applications and also using test clocks to validate your subscription logic. If you're interested in getting the code for this application, well, I'm going to have that in the link below inside of the description. Also, if you want to learn more about usagebased billing, about Stripe, and some of our different APIs, definitely make sure you check out our documentation and some of the other videos that are available here on the Stripe Developers YouTube channel. [Music]

metadata.author: Stripe Developers

Stripe and Metronome just launched billing for LLM tokens in public preview, and Stripe engineering manager Kimberly Hou walks through exactly how it works.
If your AI app calls multiple models and their prices keep changing, this is how you stop worrying about margins.

In this video, Kimberly Hou explains why pricing AI usage is so hard when customer usage varies and model prices change, then demos the full flow in a Metronome sandbox. She builds a rate card with her chosen models, sets a markup, and uses custom pricing units to bill customers in credits. metadata.title: Make Your AI Chatbot Pay For Itself — Stripe Usage Metering, Paywalls & Caps (Chat Data)
metadata.author: Medical Chat
metadata.shortDescription:
Every reply your AI chatbot sends costs you money — tokens, compute, heavier models. Left alone, one bot can quietly run up a few hundred dollars a month, and it only climbs. So what if that same chatbot could pay for itself — or become a real revenue stream?

That's Chat Data's Stripe usage metering: from one settings page you can charge for usage, cap it, or paywall the chat — all running on YOUR own connected Stripe account (one-click OAuth, no API keys, Chat Data never touches the money). Three switches — charge, cap, paywall — power everything below.

Four real-world ways to use it (escalating to the big one):

• Paid expert bot — give visitors a couple of free answers, then an in-chat "Subscribe to continue" card opens a pre-filled Stripe checkout and unlocks the bot.
• Pay-as-you-go — charge per message or by credits, add volume tiers so heavy users get a better rate, and Stripe auto-invoices each customer once they subscribe.
• Cost control (no billing) — you can meter usage without charging a cent: set a cap per customer or for the whole bot, get warning emails along the way, and the bot stops with your message at the limit. No runaway bills.
• Agencies reselling — build a chatbot for a client, connect Stripe, and it auto-bills them every month. Do it for ten clients and that's ten recurring invoices landing monthly, completely hands-off. Build once, get paid on autopilot.

Enforced on every channel — a rich subscribe card in the website widget, streamed chat and voice; the same message with a Stripe payment link as text on WhatsApp, Messenger and more.

The result: a chatbot that went from a few-hundred-dollar cost center to a profit center — or, if you'd rather, a budget that can never blow up.

Available on the Standard plan and above.

1:50 Use case 3 · Caps & cost control
2:12 Use case 4 · Agencies (recurring revenue)
2:34 Enforced on every channel
2:43 Cost center to profit center
2:57 Get started

metadata.title: AWS Activate 2026: Get Up to $200K in Credits (Org ID Explained)
metadata.author: XRaise
metadata.shortDescription:
AWS Activate gives startups between $1,000 and $200,000 in AWS credits — and one thing decides which end you land on: the Org ID. I'm Adrian from XRaise, and this is the 2026 walkthrough of both packages, where an Org ID comes from, and how to apply step by step.


🔎 Find every startup credit, perk and accelerator you qualify for: https://xraise.ai/perks?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=aws_activate&utm_content=description

⏱️ Chapters
0:00 Most AWS Activate videos are out of date
0:27 Are you eligible? AWS's 4 requirements
0:57 The two packages: Activate Founders vs Activate Portfolio
1:28 Where an Org ID comes from (Activate Providers)
2:04 How to apply in 4 steps
2:33 Why Portfolio applications get declined
2:52 After approval: expiration date & budget alerts
3:14 Recap: which package is yours
3:34 Next: AI credits (Deepgram, Anthropic, OpenAI, NVIDIA)

✅ AWS Activate in 2026, in short
• Eligibility: pre-Series B, founded in the last 10 years, AWS account on the paid plan, and new to Activate credits (or asking for more than before).
• Activate Founders (self-funded / bootstrapped): start with $1,000 in credits; select startups can qualify for up to $5,000. Apply directly.
• Activate Portfolio (backed by an accelerator, angel or VC): up to $200,000 — you need an Org ID from an AWS Activate Provider.
• Above Portfolio: AWS Credits for AI Startups, invite-only for startups ready to scale.
• How to apply: 1) create an AWS Builder ID with your professional email, 2) choose Founders or Portfolio, 3) answer questions about your product, funding stage and company, 4) create or link your AWS account and submit. AWS says you'll hear back within 5–10 business days.
• Most common Portfolio decline: AWS can't confirm you're connected to the provider whose Org ID you used. Use the exact company details your provider has on file.

✉️ The one email to send your investor or accelerator:
"Are you an AWS Activate Provider, and can you send me your Org ID or an invite?"

📚 Sources (official)
AWS Activate credits & tiers: https://aws.amazon.com/startups/credits
AWS Activate FAQ: https://aws.amazon.com/startups/faq
Amounts and terms change — always confirm on AWS before you apply.

About XRaise: XRaise helps founders find startup credits, perks and accelerators — and keeps the numbers current. XRaise is not affiliated with or endorsed by Amazon Web Services. AWS and AWS Activate are trademarks of Amazon.com, Inc. or its affiliates.

#AWSActivate #StartupCredits #XRaise

I'm Adrian from X-rays, and today I'll show you both AWS Activate packages, where an org ID actually comes from, and how to apply, step-by-step. First, >> [music] >> are you even eligible? AWS lists four things. You're pre-series B, your company was founded in the last 10 years, your AWS account is on the paid plan, [music] not the free plan, and you're either new to Activate credits, or you're asking for more than you got before. If you're a US startup, set this up with your company email on your company domain. AWS asks for details about your product, your [music] funding stage, and your company, and a professional email makes that easy. Now, the two packages. [music] Package one is called Activate Founders. It's for bootstrapped or self-funded startups. [music] You apply directly, and AWS says you start with $1,000 in credits, and select startups can qualify for more, up to $5,000. Package two [music] is Activate Portfolio. This is the one that goes up to $200,000, [music] but you can't just ask for it. You need an org ID from an Activate provider. And above that, there's an invite-only tier for startups that are ready to scale. So, where does an org ID come from? An Activate provider is an accelerator, an angel investor, or a venture firm that's part of the AWS network. AWS says there are thousands of them, [music] and names Andreessen Horowitz, Sequoia, Greylock, and Y Combinator as examples, along [music] with Brex and Carta. metadata.author: Neta Arbel | Growthgrid
metadata.shortDescription:
If your startup already received cloud credits and you want to know whether you can ask for more, start with the evidence.

Providers and cloud partners do not look at credits like a coupon. They look for a commercial case: real company stage, meaningful cloud spend, prior credit usage, a growth trigger, and provider fit.

This video walks through the five signals that decide whether another credit route, a credit extension, discounts, payment terms, funded work, or migration support may be realistic.

Check your route:
https://cloudcredits.co/

Commercial route checker:
https://cloudcredits.co/cloud-commercial-route-checker/

03:57 signal 3: credit history
05:28 signal 4: growth trigger
06:03 provider fit beats credit shopping
07:25 what you can get besides credits
08:27 check eligibility at CloudCredits

Covered:
- how to get more cloud credits
- startup cloud credit eligibility
- what happens after using startup credits
- cloud credit extensions
- cloud reseller credit routes
- discounts and payment terms
- funded cloud cost optimization
- migration funding
- why provider fit matters

#cloudcredits #startup #cloudcosts

metadata.author: Trapture Explains

Educational explainer. Not financial, legal or immigration advice. This is one founder's experience. Rules change, so check with your CA before you act.

Google's startup programme says up to $350,000 in credits. This video goes through what Google for Startups Cloud Program, AWS Activate and Microsoft for Startups say they offer and who qualifies, the free tiers you can use without a programme, and the categories of a small monthly bill, with illustrative round numbers, as of November 2026. No cloud is "the best"; it depends on your stage, your users and the one service you can't do without.

Chapters
0:00 Intro
0:25 The everyday problem
0:47 What the startup programmes say
3:02 Free tiers without a programme
4:09 A monthly bill, by category
5:29 Picking for the requirement, not the logo
6:17 The cost angle
7:01 Mistakes and myths
7:38 Recap

- Google for Startups Cloud Program: https://cloud.google.com/startup
- Google Cloud Free Program (Free Trial and Free Tier): https://cloud.google.com/free/docs/free-cloud-features
- AWS Activate credits: https://aws.amazon.com/startups/credits
- AWS Free Tier: https://aws.amazon.com/free/
- Microsoft for Startups: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/startups
- What is Microsoft for Startups (Microsoft Learn): https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-for-startups/
- Azure free services: https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/free-services
- Google Cloud Billing, budgets and budget alerts: https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets
Credit amounts and eligibility are as shown on each page on 9 Nov 2026. The rupee bill in the video is illustrative, not a real bill.

Google Cloud credits for startups in 2026: which tier you actually qualify for, why the $350,000 headline usually turns into $2,000, and the mistakes that stall an application.

I'm Adrian from XRaise. This is the Google for Startups Cloud Program without the hype: the three levels of credits, what counts as venture funding, how the money pays out over two years, and the order I'd apply in.

Chapters
0:00 Why $350K usually means $2K
0:13 The 3 levels of Google Cloud credits
0:40 Start tier: who gets $2,000
0:55 Funded tier: who qualifies for up to $200K
1:11 Funding that doesn't qualify
1:27 AI startups: the Gemini rule ($350K)
1:38 Year 1 vs year 2: how credits pay out
1:58 What Google Cloud credits can't pay for
2:12 3 mistakes that stall your application
2:42 Which tier to apply for
2:55 Check the current terms

Google Cloud startup credits in short (Google's published terms, Nov 2026)
• New customers: $300 in free credit, for any Google Cloud customer.
• Start tier: $2,000 for early startups with a working product, a clear business model and plans to raise venture funding.
• Funded tier: up to $200,000, or up to $350,000 for AI startups, with verifiable funding from pre-seed to Series A. A Series A must be from the last 12 months.
• Doesn't qualify for the funded tier: private equity, bank loans, government innovation programs, grants, crowdfunding, friends and family money.
• AI amount: for startups that use or plan to use Gemini as a foundation of their main product.
• Year 1: credits cover 100% of usage, up to $100,000 (up to $250,000 for AI startups). Year 2: 20% of usage, up to another $100,000.
• Not covered: third-party services, Google Cloud Marketplace purchases and third-party models.

Before you apply
1. Use a business email that matches your website domain and the domain on your billing account. A personal Gmail won't work.
2. Double-check your 18-character billing account ID. Credits land in the account you select.
3. Have public links that show your funding. In stealth? Your investor can verify it for you.

Official sources
Google for Startups Cloud Program: https://cloud.google.com/startup
Benefits and tiers: https://cloud.google.com/startup/benefits
FAQ: https://cloud.google.com/startup/faq
Google changes these qualifications every year and acceptance is at Google's discretion, so confirm the current terms before you apply.

metadata.title: I got $400k Cloud Credits for my AI SaaS Startup
metadata.author: Harshith Vaddiparthy
metadata.shortDescription:
The rejection highlights a common fear in the AI sector: the risk of commoditization. With the rapid pace of innovation, there is intense competition and a "race to the bottom" focused on optimizing price versus performance. For Zavata to succeed, we need a unique productization strategy that sets us apart from our competitors. Established players like Workable and HireVue have advantages due to their existing partnerships and distribution networks.

Despite these challenges, the startup credits we've secured are a vital resource that will enable us to develop and refine Zavata. These credits will allow us to leverage powerful cloud platforms and customer support tools, helping us build a differentiated product that addresses specific customer needs.

As a bootstrapped business, it's crucial to make every opportunity count. While facing uncertainty and risks, I'm also considering taking on consulting clients to ensure cash flow and sustain the business. Creating cold email automation to acquire clients, booking meetings, and utilizing tools like Slack for communication could help achieve this goal.

Entrepreneurship is often a lonely journey, filled with highs and lows. It's challenging to work in isolation, and there's always the question of whether I can truly be called an entrepreneur without a steady cash flow. However, I believe in Zavata and am determined to navigate these challenges. With perseverance, creativity, and the right resources, I am optimistic about finding our niche in the AI landscape and making Zavata a success.

metadata.shortDescription:
Google for Startups Cloud Program explained: three tracks, credits, and how to apply.
Learn how the Google for Startups Cloud Program works, from the starter credit to the early-stage track. This video walks through the three tracks, the extras beyond credits, and a five-step look at how founders apply. Whether you are pre-funded, raising a seed round, or building with AI, you will see where to start and what to check on the official page. Every figure comes from the sources listed below, and amounts can vary by cohort and region.
CHAPTERS
0:00 Google Cloud Credits Preview
0:20 Who This Is For
0:45 Three Tracks Explained
1:27 The Starter Credit
2:09 Extras Beyond Credits
2:51 How To Apply
3:33 Early-Stage Track
4:15 Quick Recap
4:40 Your Next Step
POINTS COVERED
Three tracks by funding stage, and one guide's note that the program takes no equity
Starter credit for pre-funded startups
Extras beyond credits: product credits, mentoring, and community
How to apply in five steps
Early-stage track: up to $200,000, and up to $350,000 for AI-first startups
SOURCES USED
Google for Startups Cloud Program: https://cloud.google.com/startup
Rho, Google Cloud credits: https://www.rho.co/blog/google-cloud-credits
Stackmatix, Google for Startups: https://www.stackmatix.com/blog/google-for-startups
YOUR NEXT STEP
Open Google's startup page, find the track that matches your stage, and check the current eligibility. If this video helped, like it and subscribe for more practical startup guidance.
For general information only, not financial advice. Program amounts, terms, and eligibility can change and may vary by cohort and region, so confirm details on the official page before you apply. This channel is not affiliated with Google.
Keywords
Main: Google for Startups Cloud Program
Secondary: Google Cloud credits for startups · startup cloud credits · Google Cloud startup program · AI startup credits · Google Cloud startup tracks
Long-tail: how to apply for Google for Startups Cloud Program · how much Google Cloud credit can a startup get · does Google for Startups take equity · what is the Google for Startups pre-funded track · how to get Google Cloud credits for an AI startup

Fact-check notes
Three tracks, amounts, stages: Early stage ($200,000, or up to $350,000 for AI-first, seed to Series A), pre-funded ($2,000), Series B+ (customized support). Source: Google, cloud.google.com/startup, tracks table and headline ("up to $350,000 if you're Seed to Series A").
$2,000 starter credit, valid 12 months; Skills Boost training credits, startup perks, Workspace discounts; "hasn't taken institutional funding": Source: Rho, "Start Tier" and "Eligibility" sections. Rho calls the tiers Start and Scale, while Google's page uses Pre-funded and Early stage. The script follows Google's names.
Credits used over two years; dedicated startup success manager; enhanced technical support: Source: Rho, "Scale Tier" and "Duration."
Google reviews applications and assigns the track: Source: Rho, "Tips for applying."
Program takes no equity; product credits (Workspace, Maps Platform); mentorship; technical guidance; community; five application steps; referral can speed admission, not required; amounts vary by cohort and region: Source: Stackmatix, "Additional benefits," "How to apply," and the eligibility and referral notes. These come from a single secondary source, so verify them on Google's own terms before publishing.
Application steps come from a guide, not Google's page: Google's apply page redirected to a sign-in screen, so I couldn't read it. Confirm the real steps by opening the application yourself.
NOT IN SOURCES (Google's own page): credit duration, which products the credits cover, and what counts as "AI-first." The script says "check if you qualify" instead.
Left out of the script on purpose; check before publishing: Rho lists extra eligibility rules, such as company age limits, a recent Series A, and prior Google Cloud credit history. Stackmatix says "pre-seed" can qualify, while Google's page says "seed to Series A." If you mention eligibility on screen, use Google's wording.

segments.text: Prompt caching can significantly improve the speed and cost effectiveness of large language
models. Sounds good. Sign me up. But, um. But what is prompt caching? Well,
let me start by defining what prompt caching is not. So it is not regular
output focused caching. So let me give you an example of that. If you've sent in a query and
you've sent that query into, let's say, a database, maybe it's a SQL query.Well, the
database is going to process that result and give you the output here. So we've got the
result from the database lookup. Now those results they can be stored
in a cache. And when somebody else makes that same query soon, afterwards
well, we can just kind of skip the lookup and go directly to the result stored in the cache.
Great. Now let's apply this concept to an LLM. So in this case, we have an input
prompt that we've received from a user. And that input prompt is sent for processing
into a large language model. And then, the large language model is going to
process that and send back some sort of output. We'll call this the response from the
LLM. Okay. So that's pretty standard practice. But what happens if soon after another user sends
him the same prompt? Does that prompt caching mean that we can just kind of skip the LLM call and
just go directly to the cached response? No. What I'm describing here is
actually called output caching. And it's certainly something that can be done with large
language models, but it is not what prompt caching is. Prompt caching is about caching
only the input prompt. Only caching this part here so that the LLM doesn't
need to process it a second time. Now, to understand prompt caching, you need to understand
what happens when we take a large language model, an LLM, and we send
to that large language model a prompt. So this is where we are sending in a request
prompt. Now what happens here is the model computes something called key-value
pairs. So let's model that in the LLM here as KV
pairs. And it does that at every transformer layer for every token in your input.
And we can think of these key pairs as the model's internal understanding of your prompt. So
how every word relates to every other word, what context matters, what information to focus on. And
computing these, it can be a bit expensive. This is the prefilled phase that happens before the
LLM actually can generate its first token of output. So what we can
do is cache the KV pairs. So this here is where the
prompt caching actually applies. It stores these precomputed KV
pairs. Now for a simple prompt like what's the capital of France? Well, this caching
isn't going to save much time. Processing a handful of tokens that's cheap and fast you don't
need caching. But what if we structured our prompt in a little bit of a different way? So let's
consider here a prompt that we're going to build in detail. And in this prompt,
we have put a bunch of stuff. So, for example, we're going to put a big document in our context window
here. So this is a 50-page document. And then, in our prompt, we are going to ask the
large language model to summarize that document. So here is the summarize
request. So now the model has to compute KV pairs for thousands of tokens across
dozens of transformer layers, millions of operations before it can ever start generating
that response. So with prompt caching, that processing work is getting saved. Now,
later on in a new conversation or an API call, you could send that same 50-page
document followed this time by instead of asking to summarize, we just provide some kind of
different question. And the system will recognize that document prefix. It will retrieve the cached
KV pairs and then only process the new question at the end. And that's a pretty notable saving
in latency and cost. Now what kinds of things can be cached? Let's answer that question.
What can be cached? Well, I've already mentioned that you can put
documents into a prompt into the context window. So like a 50-page product manual or
a research paper or a legal contract or anything, you want to kind of ask multiple questions about
that can be stored in the cache. But another good example, and probably the most common thing that
gets cached, is the system prompt. Now, system prompts are the most common
use case, where really every chatbot has instructions that tell it how to operate. It
defines its personality and its rules and its behavior. You know, things like you're a helpful
customer service agent, blah, blah, blah. That sort of thing can be cached. And we can also put into
the cache few short examples. So when you want the model to format responses a certain way, you show
it examples. there are a bunch of other things in a prompt that could be cached as well, like
tool and function definitions and conversation history. Okay, but when does an LLM
know what gets cached? Well, it comes down to a
technique called prefix matching to figure out what should actually be
stored in the cache. So the cache system matches your prompt from the very beginning. Token by
token. And when it encounters the first token that differs from what's cached, then caching stops and
normal processing takes over. And that makes prompt structure important for automatic caching.
So let's consider a prompt structure. Let's say that we've got a prompt that has in it some
system instructions. And then, we're going to put a document in as well. Let's say there's some kind
of 20-page manual that's here. And then, yeah, we're going to include some few shot examples as
well. And then finally we're going to submit a user question. So the user question might
be like what are the warranty terms. Am I going to use this manual to figure out the answer. Well,
this structure puts all of the static content first. So when the next request comes in with
just a different question, like now it's going to say what's the return policy? The cache matches
through all of this static content here. All of this stuff is actually
inside of the cache. And we only need to process the new question at the end.
But if we were to flip this around and we were to put the dynamic stuff first, put the question up
here, then the cache is going to fail immediately when the question changes. You'd have to reprocess
everything here again, so it's best to put that stuff up front specifically when we're talking
about automatic prompt caching So that's what gets cached. But a couple of other notes based on
prompt caching that we should talk about. One is like how much stuff to get cashed. Well, typically,
you need at least 1024 tokens to initiate
cashing. That's really before cashing provides any benefit. Because below that threshold, the overhead
of managing the cash really exceeds the savings. And also cashes don't last forever. They're
usually cleared after 5 to 10 minutes just to keep the data fresh. Although
some can hang around for up to 24 hours. And some providers provide the automatic caching that I've
been talking about here. But some providers actually require you to explicitly mark
which parts of your prompt should be cached in your API calls. So these are the explicit types of
caching. So, so, that's prompt caching. And with the right use case it's a way to
reduce LLM costs and latency.

metadata.title: Stop Wasting AI Tokens: The Ultimate LLM Cost Reduction Guide (Save 90%!)
metadata.author: The Macroscope
metadata.shortDescription:
How to Reduce LLM API Costs by 10x | Token Optimization & Prompt Compression
Are your LLM API bills spiraling out of control? 💸 Token management is the silent cost killer in every AI workflow In this video, we dive deep into the token economy and reveal practical strategies to reduce your LLM costs by up to 90% without sacrificing response quality.
Whether you are building with OpenAI's GPT-4o, Anthropic's Claude, or open-source models, treating token optimization as a core AI engineering skill is essential for scalability. From writing smarter prompts to implementing advanced compression frameworks, we cover everything you need to know!

📌 What you will learn in this video:
Smart Prompt Design: How to write imperative instructions and avoid the "verbose trap" to save input tokens.
Prompt Compression: Using tools like Microsoft's LLMLingua to compress prompts by up to 20x while retaining semantic integrity.
Data Format Optimization: Why JSON is secretly draining your token budget and how lightweight formats like TOON (Token-Oriented Object Notation) or YAML can cut your payload size by 30-60%.
Caching & Routing: How to use Prompt Caching for static prefixes and implement Cascading Model Routing to send simple tasks to cheaper models (like GPT-4o-mini or Haiku).
Output Discipline: Controlling LLM verbosity using hard levers like max_tokens and stop sequences.

metadata.title: Prompt Caching & Cost Optimization for AI Agents | Reduce LLM Cost & Latency
metadata.author: AmanAI Lab
metadata.shortDescription:
Prompt Caching & Cost Optimization for AI Agents | Reduce LLM Cost & Latency

How do you reduce LLM costs and latency in production AI Agents?

In this video, we'll understand Prompt Caching, Semantic Caching, Token Optimization, and other cost-optimization techniques used when building production-ready LLM and Agentic AI applications.

As AI Agents make multiple LLM calls, costs can increase quickly because the same instructions, tools, context, and documents may be sent repeatedly. Prompt caching and semantic caching can help reduce unnecessary computation and improve application performance.

In this video, I explain these concepts practically and show how they fit into a real-world Agentic AI architecture.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🎯 WHAT YOU'LL LEARN

✅ What is Prompt Caching?
✅ Why Prompt Caching is important for AI Agents
✅ How Prompt Caching works
✅ Prompt Cache vs Semantic Cache
✅ What should be stored in a Semantic Cache?
✅ How caching reduces LLM cost
✅ How caching improves latency
✅ Token optimization techniques
✅ Context optimization for Agents
✅ Reducing unnecessary LLM calls
✅ Cache invalidation strategies
✅ What happens when RAG documents change?
✅ Efficient handling of small document changes
✅ Cost optimization for RAG systems
✅ Cost optimization for Agentic AI
✅ Production considerations for LLM caching

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

⏱️ TIMESTAMPS

00:00 – Introduction
00:20 – What is Prompt Caching?
01:07 – How Prompt Caching works
04:29 – Optimization Technique
13:40 - Coding Prompt Caching and Cost Optimization

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🧠 PROMPT CACHING

Prompt caching is useful when the same or repeated context is sent to an LLM multiple times.

For example, an AI Agent may repeatedly send:

System Instructions
+
Agent Rules
+
Tool Definitions
+
Large Context
+
User Query

Instead of processing everything from scratch every time, caching mechanisms can reduce repeated processing and improve efficiency.

This becomes especially useful for:

🔹 AI Agents
🔹 Long System Prompts
🔹 Tool-Calling Agents
🔹 RAG Applications
🔹 Multi-Agent Systems
🔹 Long-Context Applications

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

⚡ SEMANTIC CACHING

Semantic caching works differently.

Instead of checking whether the exact same query was received, we can compare the meaning of the new query with previous queries.

For example:

Query 1:
"What is the refund policy?"

Query 2:
"How can I get my money back?"

These queries are different strings but may have similar meanings.

A semantic cache can store:

🔹 User query
🔹 Query embedding
🔹 Generated response
🔹 Relevant metadata
🔹 Model/configuration information
🔹 Document/version information when required

If a new query is sufficiently similar to a previous query, we can potentially return the cached response instead of making another LLM call.

📚 RAG + CACHING

One important production question is:

"What happens if my RAG document changes slightly?"

You don't necessarily want to rebuild and reprocess the entire knowledge base every time a small change occurs.

A more efficient approach can involve:

Document Versioning
↓
Content Hashing
↓
Identify Changed Sections/Chunks
↓
Re-embed Only Changed Content
↓
Update Vector Store
↓
Invalidate Affected Cache Entries

This allows the system to update only what has actually changed instead of unnecessarily processing everything again.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🤖 COST OPTIMIZATION FOR AI AGENTS

AI Agents can make multiple LLM calls during a single task.

For example:

User
↓
Planner
↓
Research Agent
↓
Tool Call
↓
Analysis Agent
↓
Final Response

If every step uses a large model and sends a large context, the cost can increase significantly.

Optimization strategies include:

🔹 Use smaller models where appropriate
🔹 Cache repeated prompts
🔹 Cache reusable responses
🔹 Reduce unnecessary context
🔹 Avoid duplicate tool calls
🔹 Limit unnecessary Agent iterations
🔹 Use structured outputs
🔹 Optimize retrieval
🔹 Monitor token usage
🔹 Track cost per Agent
