metadata.title: Why Your Claude Code Limit Vanishes: Cut AI Coding Costs by 70% with Cache & Model Routing
metadata.author: Spec & Ship
metadata.shortDescription:
Why does one developer hit the 5-hour Claude Code usage limit in 40 minutes while another ships 6 complex pull requests on the exact same plan?

In this breakdown, we cover the quadratic cost of long chat threads, how 90% KV prefix caching works under the hood, the 3 silent habits that invalidate your prompt cache, surgical line-range file reads, Planner-Worker model routing, and subagent context garbage collection.

Watch Episode #01 (The 5-Step Spec & Review Workflow): https://youtu.be/sDj89WxjWjQ
Watch Episode #02 (The 60-Line CLAUDE.md Architecture): https://youtu.be/dNzaKe-PRSA

Chapters:
0:00 The 3:00 Pm Limit Lockout
0:30 The Quadratic Chat Cost Curve
1:00 The 90% Prompt Cache Discount
1:34 Never Put Timestamps In Claude.Md
2:01 Mid-Session Tool & Model Swaps
2:30 The 5-Minute Cache Ttl Clock
2:59 Surgical Line-Range Reads
3:27 Planner Vs. Worker Model Routing
3:56 Silencing Verbose Cli Logs
4:20 Subagents As Garbage Collectors
4:46 Hard /Clear Between Slices
5:10 The Complete Spec & Ship System

#claudecode #promptcaching #aicoding #contextengineering #softwareengineering #cursor

segments.text: Put two engineers on the exact same
repository with the exact same
subscription plan or API budget.
Engineer A hits the five hour usage
lockout after 40 minutes or racks up $80
in API charges before lunch. Engineer B
ships six complex pull requests all day
long and barely touches 30% of their
quota. The difference is not how fast
they type. It is how they engineer
prompt caching, prefix stability, and
model routing.
First, understand the math of a
multi-turn coding session. Large
language models are stateless. On turn
one, you send 10,000 tokens. On turn
two, you resend those 10,000 tokens plus
the new file read. By turn 40 of a
debugging thread, every single one-line
reply resends 160,000
tokens of accumulated history. Without
prompt caching and session resets,
cumulative token cost grows
quadratically with turn count.
Modern model APIs solve this with
key-value prefix caching where cached
input tokens cost up to 90% less than
fresh input tokens. Here is the catch. A
KV cache is an exact byte-for-byte
prefix match from the very top of the
prompt downward. Your system prompt is
layer one, tool schemas are layer two,
cloud.md is layer three, and chat
history is layer four. If a single byte
changes in layer two, every layer below
it is invalidated and billed at full
price.
That brings us to the number one cache
killer, dynamic text in your root
prompt. Some developers configure hooks
that inject the current timestamp,
random session IDs, or live git status
into the top of their system
instructions on every turn. Because that
top string changes every second, it
invalidates the entire 100,000 token
prefix cache on every single message.
Keep your top prefix
static.
Cache killer number two is toggling MCP
servers or switching models mid thread.
Tool definitions sit right at the bottom
of your system prompt above your entire
conversation history.
If you enable or disable an MCP server
on turn 25 or flip back and forth
between two different model families
inside the same chat, you force a full
uncached cold read of the entire thread.
Instead, spawn a sub agent when you need
a different model or tool set.
Cache killer number three is the five
minute ephemeral TTL clock. Standard
prompt caches stay warm in GPU memory
for five minutes after your last turn.
If you have a massive 140,000 token
session, walk away for 10 minutes to
grab coffee and then type now fix the
button style. Your cache has expired and
that tiny follow up pays full price to
reencode the entire history.
Run slash clear before starting a new
task after a break.
Now let's cut how fast your context
fills up in the first place.
When an unguided agent looks for a bug,
it often reads five entire files,
dumping 8,000 lines of code into your
prompt.
Add a surgical read rule to your 60 line
claw.md. Always grep for symbol and line
number first, then read only a 50 to 80
line window around the match. You cut
file read token ingestion by 85%.
Next is planner worker model routing.
Frontier reasoning models cost up to
five times more per token than fast
coding models.
Use your flagship frontier model for 10
minutes to interview you, resolve edge
cases, and write the explicit 50 line
markdown spec.
Once the spec lists exact files, types,
and test assertions, hand execution of
the vertical slices to your fast coding
model, which executes unambiguous specs
at a fraction of the cost. Another
silent budget drain is terminal standout
pollution. Every time your agent runs
npm install, Docker build, or a full
test suite without quiet flags,
thousands of lines of progress bars and
deprecation warnings get appended
permanently to your chat context. Wrap
your build and test commands in scripts
that pass dash dash silent and only
print standout when a command actually
fails.
Think of sub agents as automatic memory
garbage collection for LLM context.
Every token added to your main chat
stays there for the rest of the session,
getting rebuild on every turn. Every
token spent inside a sub agent is
temporary. The moment the sub agent
returns its 10-line answer and
terminates, its 40,000 tokens of
exploratory file reads are garbage
collected for good.
The single highest leverage habit for
token efficiency is running slash clear
the second a git commit lands. Never
carry 30,000 tokens of dead debugging
history from slice one into slice two.
Because your progress lives on disk in
spec.md and git log, resetting your
context drops your per-turn token
footprint from 120,000 tokens back down
Over these first six episodes of Spec
and Ship, you have seen the complete
production engineering harness. Spec
first vertical slices, the 60-line
claw.md router, the five high ROI MCP
servers, parallel git work trees,
four-ring self-healing verification
loops, and prefix cache cost
engineering. Subscribe to Spec and Ship,
drop your toughest workflow question in
the comments, and go ship clean code.

metadata.title: How Prompt Caching makes LLM calls 10x Cheaper
metadata.author: cruxbits8
metadata.shortDescription:
Send the same request twice. The second time can cost one tenth as much — same model, same answer.

This video breaks down prompt caching: how the model stores an already-processed prompt prefix and drops it back in instead of re-reading it — following one example (a 200,000-token handbook) all the way through the math.

You'll learn:
• Prefix reuse — why the model normally re-reads your entire prompt on every call, and how caching skips it
• The pricing asymmetry — cached reads at 1/10th the normal input rate, one-time writes at 1.25x (it pays for itself after a single hit)
• How to turn it on — one cache-control marker, up to 4 cache points, tools → system → conversation order
• The 5-minute lifetime that resets on every hit, and the ~1,000-token minimum
• Why multi-turn conversations compound the savings — the cache point slides forward, so nearly every later token is a cheap read
• The bonus: it's faster too — a cached call dropping from ~5 seconds to under 1

#PromptCaching #LLM #AIEngineering #ClaudeAPI #AICost

metadata.title: How I cut token costs by 90%: AI cost optimization guide
metadata.author: ClankerEngineer
metadata.shortDescription:
I cut a startup's LLM token costs by 90%, saving them over $1 million a year. If you are an AI engineer struggling with expensive RAG pipelines or high API latency, this optimization guide will help you stop burning tokens. 

I walk you through implementing Cloudflare AI Gateway for intelligent caching, replacing pricey LLM-as-a-judge workflows with open-source re-ranker models (like bge-reranker-base), and using LangGraph SummarizationNode to compress chat history context. We also dive into Python-based prompt routing, reducing dimensions of vector embeddings, and the undocumented quirks of OpenAI Prefix Caching, giving you everything you need to build fast, scalable, and cost-effective AI agents.

Need career advice, a mock interview or resume review for an AI engineer role? Work with me 1:1:
https://clankerengineer.io/book

My #1 AI tool:
https://ref.wisprflow.ai/gustaf

Sign up for my newsletter where I share what I learn as a senior AI engineer:
https://the-human-loop.beehiiv.com/

50 Advanced Python Concepts to get a Senior Developer Job in 2026:
https://youtu.be/QgC5lj54TNg

Day in the life of a Senior AI Engineer in Stockholm, Sweden:
https://youtu.be/ZjyibllzdNo

How I contribute to open source to get highly-paid AI engineer jobs:
https://youtu.be/hcoO-MDRKyc

Uh this is just another API call to get these, and these secrets should be cached as well, um which also reduced the latency a lot. So, this all ended up in a much cheaper and much faster application. [music] And this means you can use something called prefix caching, which I think OpenAI has done a horrible job of documenting cuz it's such an underrated feature. So, what you need to do is uh take a look at your system prompt. metadata.author: Engineering Insider
metadata.shortDescription:
Building an AI app is easy. Scaling it without burning money is the real challenge.

In this video, we break down the hidden costs of modern AI applications and explain how startups can control LLM spending while maintaining performance. You will learn why redundant API calls, long system prompts, inefficient model usage, and poor infrastructure design can quickly destroy your unit economics.

We also explore practical optimization strategies such as semantic caching, provider-level prompt caching, model routing, rate limiting, and cost-aware architecture. These techniques can help reduce AI operating costs dramatically and turn an expensive chatbot into a sustainable AI product.

This guide is perfect for AI engineers, startup founders, SaaS builders, developers, and anyone building production-grade AI applications.

What You Will Learn

↳ Why LLM applications become expensive quickly
↳ How redundant API calls waste money
↳ Why long prompts increase token costs
↳ How semantic caching reduces repeated inference
↳ How provider-level prompt caching can cut costs
↳ How model routing sends simple tasks to cheaper models
↳ Why rate limiting protects your budget
↳ How to balance AI performance with financial viability
↳ How to design sustainable AI unit economics

AI Costs Are Killing Startups
Stop Burning LLM Tokens
Build Cheaper AI Apps
LLM Cost Optimization

#AIEngineering #LLM #GenerativeAI #StartupAI #PromptCaching #ModelRouting #AIInfrastructure #ArtificialIntelligence #SaaS #OpenAI #ClaudeAI #GeminiAI #AIOptimization #MachineLearning

metadata.title: Prompt Caching Reduced My Agent Costs by 90%
metadata.author: Mastra
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn how to cut your Mastra agent's input token costs by up to 90% and latency by up to 80% with prompt caching. In this video, @bookercodes at Mastra teaches you how to structure your prompts so the savings actually fire in production agents... and what most developers get wrong.

You'll learn what triggers a cache hit, what silently invalidates one, and how to lay out your prompt to keep caches warm across long agent loops.

🔗 MENTIONED IN THE VIDEO
ProjectDiscovery blog — How we cut LLM costs by 59%: https://projectdiscovery.io/blog/how-we-cut-llm-cost-with-prompt-caching
OpenAI prompt caching docs: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching
Anthropic prompt caching docs: https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-caching

📚 MASTRA RESOURCES
Website: https://mastra.ai
X: https://x.com/mastra_ai
Discord: https://mastra.ai/community/discord
GitHub: https://github.com/mastra-ai
Course: https://mastra.ai/course
Principles of Building AI Agents: https://mastra.ai/books/principles-of-building-ai-agents
Patterns of Building AI Agents: https://mastra.ai/books/patterns-of-building-ai-agents

WHAT IS MASTRA?
Mastra is an open-source TypeScript framework designed for building and shipping AI-powered applications and agents with minimal friction. It supports the full lifecycle of agent development — from prototype to production.

00:00 Intro
00:30 Prompt caching fundamentals
01:30 Demo
02:19 The exact prefix rule
02:54 Case study: ProjectDiscovery
03:13 Optimization Techniques
04:35 Your prompt as a series of blocks
05:47 Recap

metadata.title: Why agents recompute the same prompt, and how prompt caching fixes it
metadata.author: Efficient NLP
metadata.shortDescription:
Prompt caching is how agents avoid recomputing the same prompt prefix on every turn. I explain what it is, how to keep your agent's prompts cache-friendly, and what servers do behind the scenes to route and store the KV cache efficiently.

0:00 - Introduction
0:46 - What is prompt caching?
2:50 - Optimizing for cache hits
4:04 - Cache-aware server routing
5:03 - Anthropic vs OpenAI cache mechanisms
5:52 - Automatic caching with radix attention
7:49 - Prompt caching security

My KV Cache video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=80bIUggRJf4
Claude prompt caching docs: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching
"Don't Break the Cache" (Lumer et al., 2026): https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06007
KV-Cache Wins You Can See (llm-d): https://llm-d.ai/blog/kvcache-wins-you-can-see
SGLang / RadixAttention (Zheng et al., 2024): https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.07104
Auditing Prompt Caching in LM APIs (Gu et al., 2025): https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.07776

metadata.title: How Prompt Caching Saves 90% (GPT-6 Astra) – Cut Your LLM API Bill
metadata.author: Learn with Vichu
metadata.shortDescription:
Two coding agents. Same model. Same task. Both use the prompt cache. One costs $123, the other $24. The difference is one number in the config.

In this video, we work out exactly how prompt caching on OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra cuts your input bill by up to 90%, with real numbers from a few thousand tokens to millions.

You will learn:
• Why the same 1M tokens cost $10 the first time and $1 the next
• Why cache writes cost more than normal input, and caching still saves 90%
• Why one timestamp at the top of your prompt kills the cache
• Why one extra token past 272K can double the price of the whole request
• Why compacting (summarizing) too often raises your bill instead of cutting it
• When to compact a long-running agent
• 9 best practices to get high cache hit rates in production

⏱️ Chapters
0:00 Hook: $123 vs $24
0:55 The context window
1:34 The price list
2:24 The model has no memory
3:05 Our prompt
3:53 10 turns without the cache
4:38 10 turns with the cache
5:31 Inside: the KV cache
6:15 The prefix rule
7:08 Breakpoints, routing and lifetime
8:17 Reading the usage block
8:54 Break-even: when caching pays off
9:42 One million tokens
10:31 Millions of tokens: a long agent
11:18 Compaction and the cache
13:03 Best practices 1–5
14:05 Best practices 6–9
14:52 Claude and Gemini
15:26 Recap

💰 GPT-6 Astra prices used (per 1M tokens)
Input $10 · Cached input $1 · Cache write $12.50 (30 min) / $25 (12 h) · Output $50
Above 272K input tokens: input and cache ×2, output ×1.5

📚 Links
OpenAI prompt caching guide: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching
OpenAI API pricing: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing
GPT-6 Astra model page: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6-astra
OpenAI compaction guide: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/compaction
OpenAI conversation state: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/conversation-state
Anthropic Claude prompt caching: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching
Google Gemini context caching: https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/caching

Note: prices are from OpenAI's docs as of October 2026. Check the pricing page for current rates. The coding-agent costs (150 turns, +5,000 tokens per turn, 10K summary) come from a simple cost model at these rates.

#PromptCaching #OpenAI #LLM

metadata.title: How KV Cache Speeds Up LLMs for Faster AI Models on GPUs
metadata.author: IBM Technology
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn more about LLM inference here → https://ibm.biz/~Ewjm0UejN

Why do LLMs crawl when traffic spikes? 🤔 Legare Kerrison explains how KV cache and paged attention reshape GPU memory across prefill and decode to speed up LLM inference. Learn how smarter context handling unlocks faster AI models, lower latency, and better GPU throughput. 🚀

AI news moves fast. Sign up for a monthly newsletter for AI updates from IBM → https://ibm.biz/~nnmLUPhCs

#llm #aiinfrastructure #gpu #machinelearning

With one user, time to first token is super quick.
And at 10 users, we're starting to see latency climb.
But then at a hundred, you're watching GPU memory spike and throughput tank.
And every cycle is wasted money.
Your model is most likely not the culprit here, but rather how your memory is being used during inference.
Specifically how the model stores and retrieves the context it's building token by token.
Today, we're going to unpack two mechanisms for reducing wait time and cost associated with inferencing models.
They are KV cache.
And paged attention.
They both come out of the open source inference engine, VLLM.
And they've helped us make strides in what's possible for LLMs that we are inferencing at scale.
Now, by the end of this video, you'll know exactly how these two techniques work,
why they work, and how you can configure them to get dramatically more
throughput out of a GPU that you already have.
If you've used an LLM API, you've noticed this.
You'll submit a long prompt and then wait for a bit.
Then suddenly tokens will stream back fast.
That lag before your first token is the model processing your prompt.
This is the pre-fill phase.
It's one of the two phases in LLM inferencing, and it's highly compute bound.
This is where the model has to run your input through every transformer layer to
build a mathematical representation of everything you said before it can produce a single output token.
Now, imagine that you're doing this for those 100 simultaneous users.
And every request has its own growing context.
And every step of token generation, the system has to reach back into GPU memory and retrieve that context.

This is Memory Bound.

Okay, now that we understand the two phases of LLM imprints, prefill, and decode, let's discuss KV cache and page detention.
When a transformer generates a new token, every layer computes three things for each token it's attending to.
A query, a value, and a key.
Now, the query is the concurrent token asking, what's relevant?
To me.
And then the key and the value are answering that question.
The problem is that in autoregressive generation, you're producing one token at a time,
but you have to rerun attention over all previous tokens on every single step.
Without a cache, generating a thousand-token response means that the thousandth token
has to recompute the keys and values for all 999 tokens before it. The KV cache just stores those keys
and value matrices from previous steps so they don't recompute what you already know.
Each new token only needs to compute its own KVQ.
Then it attends over the cached KV history.
KV cache is a memory for compute trade-off, but it's proven to be worth it for long sequences.
Memory is the real bottleneck in LLM serving.
So now let's look at how this naive serving allocates GPU memory.
So a 13 billion parameter model, something like the Llama 13B, takes
about 26 gigabytes of GPU memory just for its weights on an A140 gigabyte card.
That's already 65% of our available memory.
Just for the weights.
That's VRAM before the user hits a single endpoint.
Now, the remaining 35% has to support the KV cache for every active request.
And here's where this traditional system starts to fall apart.
They pre-allocate a fixed contiguous block of memory for each request based on the maximum possible output length.
So if your max context is 2048 tokens, but the average user sends in 200 tokens and gets 300 back,
that's 1,500 tokens of reserved memory just sitting empty per request.
So research shows that these traditional systems are wasting about 60 to 80% of
this 35% used for KV cache memory, leaving only a small bit actually usable.
While page detention treats GPU memory like OS treats RAM.
Now, the KV cache is powerful, but it creates a new problem.
How do you store it efficiently for many concurrent requests of wildly different lengths?
Traditional systems store each request KV cache as a giant contiguous block,
like reserving an entire hotel floor for a single guest.
So if your max sequence length is 2,048 tokens, that's how much memory you have on reserve.
Even if the user only generates 200 tokens, the rest is wasted and unavailable for anyone else.
And this is called internal fragmentation.
It can be the culprit for KV cache memory waste along with external fragmentation,
where a request of varying lengths leave large gaps between allocations.
So if a new request needs 500 tokens, you may very well have enough memory,
but no continuous region big enough for this to work.
Also, look out for redundant duplication where the system prompt is stored separately for every concurrent request.
Now, page attention eliminates each one of these issues and applies the exact same insight
that operating systems use for RAM, virtual memory paging.
And instead of one contiguous block, it breaks KV cache into small fixed page sizes by default, 16 tokens each.
Now these pages can live anywhere in GPU memory, non-contiguous, allocated on demand.
So a lightweight block table maps logical page addresses,
and this is what the model sees, to physical page addresses where they
actually are in VRAM so that your GPU memory allocation looks more like this.
Where you have 65% still allocated to these weights,
but then the rest of this 35%.
Finally, here are three things you can tune on your deployment to get the most out of your GPU.
First, tune GPU memory utilization.
This controls what fraction of remaining VRAM goes to KV cache.
The default is 0.9.
Push it to 0.95 on stable workloads to pack more concurrent requests and pull
it to .8 if you're seeing OOM errors under load burst.
And you can benchmark your specific model before you commit here.
If you need something to do that, you can check out guide LLM.
It's an open source part of the LLM project.
Second, enable prefix caching.
Page detention hashes each KV block by its token sequence.
Requests sharing a system prompt point to the same physical memory.
VLLM computes and stores it once.
In RAG pipelines, multi-turn chat and coding agents that are gonna hit rates of 75 to 95% are common,
with time to first token dropping dramatically because shared prefill is skipped entirely.
Third, enable chunked prefill.
For throughput heavy workloads, by default VLLM runs prefill to completion before resuming decode,
which causes streamed tokens to stutter when long prompts arrive.
Chunked prefilled batches inflate decode request first, then fills remaining compute budget with prefilled chunks.
Production deployments have seen 50% throughput improvement.
And you can also set max-num batch tokens to greater than 2048 alongside it.
Finally, a bonus feature for latency-sensitive workloads is enabling a speculative decoding model.
Speculative-model.
Now, during decode, your GPU has spare compute idle between memory reads.

Proposes a series of output tokens.

Output quality here is mathematically identical to running the large model alone.
And at very high concurrency, the gains shrink since the batch is already keeping the GPU busy.
So reach for this when interactive latency matters more than raw throughput.
The LLM also ships a zero cost Ingram speculator via dash dash speculative dash model Ingram.
And that's for structured or repetitive outputs.
I hope this was helpful, and I'd love to know what the biggest memory-related
